query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled post-casting aging treatment that induces fine Ni3Ti precipitates will improve the elevated‐temperature strength and creep resistance of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy by impeding dislocation motion.
generation.material_initial_state: A cast, homogenized high-entropy alloy where titanium and nickel represent the primary constituents (e.g., each around 30–40 at%) and at least three other elements (each 5–35 at%) are included according to high-entropy alloy criteria. The material is produced via vacuum induction melting followed by homogenization.
generation.intervention: Apply an aging heat treatment at approximately 800°C for 4 hours in a controlled inert (or vacuum) atmosphere, followed by a controlled cooling process to promote the formation of evenly dispersed, nano-scale precipitates.
generation.conditions: Testing the mechanical performance at elevated temperatures, for example, tensile and creep tests performed at around 700°C under conditions mimicking service loads (moderate strain rates or constant load, respectively).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of fine, thermally stable Ni3Ti precipitates (or a similar ordered phase) that are distributed within the matrix.
generation.mechanism: Precipitation strengthening: The induced nano-precipitates act as obstacles to dislocation motion and grain boundary sliding, thereby increasing yield strength and slowing creep deformation at elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: The aged alloy will exhibit increased yield strength and improved creep resistance at elevated temperatures relative to the as-cast/homogenized (unaged) baseline alloy.
generation.baseline: The same titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy in its as-cast or homogenized state without the post-casting aging treatment.
generation.boundary: The composition remains within the high-entropy range (each constituent within 5–35 at%) with titanium and nickel as the primary elements. The treatment temperature is approximately 800°C and the test temperature is around 700°C, appropriate for high-temperature applications. Timing of the aging (4 hours) is selected to encourage nano-scale precipitation without excessive coarsening.
generation.uncertainty: The magnitude of the mechanical improvement is uncertain and may depend on precise chemistry, aging time, and potential competing microstructural changes. There is also uncertainty regarding the uniform formation and stability of the Ni3Ti precipitates during service conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy via vacuum induction melting and homogenize them. Apply the aging treatment (800°C for 4 hours in an inert atmosphere followed by controlled cooling) to one set while keeping the other set in the as-cast/homogenized state. Conduct elevated-temperature tensile and creep tests at 700°C that mimic expected service conditions.
measurements: Microstructural analysis using TEM/SEM to assess the presence, size, and distribution of nano-scale precipitates (e.g., Ni3Ti).
Tensile testing at 700°C to measure yield strength and ultimate strength.
Creep testing at 700°C under constant load to evaluate time-to-failure and steady-state creep rates.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aged samples do not show a statistically significant improvement (for instance, less than a 10% increase in yield strength or negligible improvement in creep resistance) compared to the unaged samples, or if the intended precipitate phase is not observed, then the hypothesis is falsified.
